doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Henderson, Goodman and the swing era
title: Defining swing: Henderson's background figures and section rehearsals
summary: They talk about the syncopated horn parts, the Hendersons' background figures, and section rehearsals as in Lunceford's band.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: How about defining swing for us?
[Laughs] Oh come on man. Please tell me you are joking.

No. I’m not. But it did occur to me that with the big band the last couple of nights, playing the tunes from that era, the 30s and stuff, that the solid rhythm underneath this [scats] those horn parts are so syncopated and that the wonderful, smooth sort of tension it creates is just astounding.

Yeah, exactly. And I like the fact that if you listen to those, the little figures that Fletcher Henderson or Horace Henderson did as backgrounds to the soloists, I think they are wonderful by themselves, just listening to those background figures. They’re very nice.
And they’re really tricky to play.
It made me appreciate the arrangers and the cats that played those things.
Because sometimes you read about the fact that maybe they all weren’t great readers, but they, boy, they did that stuff so well.

Well and they also had section rehearsals I’m sure they sat down and the sections just rehearsed. I mean certainly that happened in Lunceford’s band a lot where the sections would just rehearse their parts and then when they came together, boom, they’re ready to roll. So exactly. They wanted to make sure they got it right and made it sound good.
